title: Uranus and Neptune: The Ice Giants
summary: How Uranus and Neptune, the distant blue ice giants, are built, how they behave, and how they were discovered and explored.
poll: Scientists should send a new spacecraft to visit Uranus or Neptune.

versions.title: Two Blue Planets
versions.text:
Far, far from the Sun are two blue worlds. One is Uranus. One is Neptune. Each is a planet.

Uranus is the seventh from the Sun. Neptune is the eighth. It is the last one.

Each is a giant. Put four Earths in a row. That is how wide each one is!

They are ice giants. They are full of thick, icy stuff. There is no ground. A gas in the air makes them blue.

It is so cold out there. The Sun looks like a small star.

Uranus is tilted. It spins on its side. It rolls like a ball. One end gets sun for years. Then it is dark for years.

Neptune has the fastest winds of all. They blow much faster than a jet.

A man found Uranus long ago. He used a telescope. It is a tool to see far. Then math helped find Neptune.

Each has thin rings. Each has lots of moons, too.

One ship went near them. It flew by. It sent back photos.

versions.title: The Ice Giants
versions.text:
Far beyond the other planets are two blue worlds called Uranus and Neptune. Each one is a planet in our solar system.

Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Neptune is the eighth, which makes it the farthest planet of all.

Both planets are giants. Each one is about four times as wide as Earth.

It is freezing cold so far out in space. From there, the Sun looks like a small, bright star.

Neptune has the fastest winds of any planet. They blow much faster than a jet plane can fly.

versions.title: Uranus and Neptune: The Ice Giants
versions.text:
At the cold, dark edge of our solar system, two blue worlds move slowly around the Sun. They are Uranus and Neptune, and scientists call them the ice giants.

Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, and Neptune is the eighth. Neptune is about thirty times as far from the Sun as Earth is, so its sunlight is very weak. Each of the two planets is about four times as wide as Earth.

They are called ice giants because most of their inside is made of icy stuff, such as water. Neither one has solid ground. Their air holds a gas called methane, which makes them look blue. In their clouds, it gets colder than minus 200 degrees Celsius.

Uranus is odd because it is tilted so far that it spins on its side. As it moves along its orbit, each end of the planet gets about 42 years of sunlight, followed by about 42 years of dark.

These planets have long years. It takes Uranus 84 Earth years to go once around the Sun. Neptune takes about 165 years.

Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system. They can blow at more than 2,000 kilometers an hour.

In 1781, a man named William Herschel found Uranus with a telescope. Later, people saw that Uranus was being pulled a bit off its path. They used math to guess where a new planet might be, and in 1846 Neptune was found there.

Both planets have thin rings and many moons. Neptune's biggest moon, Triton, goes around it the wrong way. Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2, has been to these worlds, flying past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

versions.text:

Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, and Neptune is the eighth. Neptune is approximately thirty times farther from the Sun than Earth is, so the sunlight that reaches it is extremely feeble. Both planets are roughly four times as wide as Earth.

They are called ice giants because most of their interior consists of icy materials such as water and ammonia, surrounding a relatively small rocky core. Neither planet has a solid surface. Their atmosphere contains methane, a gas that absorbs red light and therefore gives them their distinctive blue color, and temperatures in their clouds drop below minus 200 degrees Celsius.

Uranus is remarkable because it is tilted so dramatically that it essentially spins on its side. As the planet travels along its orbit, each pole experiences about 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by approximately 42 years of darkness.

Because they are so distant, both planets also have extremely long years: Uranus takes 84 Earth years to circle the Sun once, while Neptune requires about 165 years to complete a single journey.

Neptune has the fastest winds measured anywhere in the solar system, which can exceed 2,000 kilometers per hour.

In 1781, the astronomer William Herschel discovered Uranus with a telescope, making it the first planet found with that instrument. Later, astronomers noticed that Uranus was being tugged slightly away from its predicted path. Both planets possess faint rings and numerous moons. Neptune's largest moon, Triton, orbits in the opposite direction from the planet's rotation, which is extremely unusual for a large moon, and some scientists believe it was captured from farther out in the solar system. Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2, has ever visited these worlds, flying past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

versions.title: Distant Twins: The Ice Giants
versions.text:
At the frigid, dimly illuminated edge of our solar system, two blue worlds travel slowly around the Sun. They are Uranus and Neptune, and astronomers classify them as the ice giants, a category distinct from both rocky terrestrial planets like Earth and enormous gas giants like Jupiter.

Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, and Neptune is the eighth. Neptune is approximately thirty times farther from the Sun than Earth is, so the illumination reaching it is extremely feeble; nevertheless, both planets are roughly four times as wide as Earth itself.

They are called ice giants because most of their interior consists of icy materials such as water and ammonia, surrounding a comparatively small rocky core, and neither planet possesses any solid surface whatsoever. Their atmosphere contains methane, a gas that absorbs red light and consequently gives both planets their distinctive blue coloration, while temperatures within their swirling clouds plunge below minus 200 degrees Celsius.

Uranus is particularly remarkable because it is tilted so dramatically that it essentially rotates on its side rather than upright, a peculiarity most astronomers attribute to an ancient, cataclysmic collision early in the planet's history. As the planet travels along its lengthy orbit, each pole experiences roughly 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by approximately 42 years of uninterrupted darkness.

Because they are so remarkably distant, both planets also have extraordinarily long years: Uranus requires 84 Earth years to circle the Sun once, while Neptune requires approximately 165 years to complete a single revolution.

Neptune has the fastest winds ever measured anywhere in the entire solar system, winds that can exceed 2,000 kilometers per hour.

In 1781, the astronomer William Herschel discovered Uranus with a telescope, making it the first planet ever identified with that particular instrument. Subsequently, astronomers noticed that Uranus was being tugged slightly away from its predicted path, so they used mathematics to calculate where an undiscovered planet might be located, and in 1846 Neptune was observed almost precisely at the calculated position, a genuine triumph of careful mathematical reasoning.

Both planets possess faint rings and numerous moons. Neptune's largest moon, Triton, orbits in the opposite direction from the planet's rotation, which is extraordinarily unusual for a large moon, and many scientists believe it was captured from farther out in the solar system. Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2, has ever visited them, flying past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, and much of what scientists understand about these remote worlds still originates from that single, extraordinary expedition.

versions.title: Distant Twins: The Ice Giants
versions.text:
At the frigid, dimly illuminated outer edge of our entire solar system, two distant blue worlds travel slowly and silently around the Sun, almost imperceptibly to any observer. They are Uranus and Neptune, and astronomers formally classify them as the ice giants, a distinct category entirely separate from both rocky terrestrial planets such as Earth and the enormous gas giants exemplified by Jupiter and Saturn.

Uranus is the seventh planet outward from the Sun, and Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet currently recognized. Neptune lies approximately thirty times farther from the Sun than Earth does, so the sunlight eventually reaching its distant surface is extraordinarily feeble by the time it arrives, and both planets measure roughly four times as wide as Earth across their respective equators.

They are designated ice giants precisely because the overwhelming majority of their interior mass consists of icy materials such as water and ammonia, all surrounding a relatively small rocky core situated at the very center, and neither planet possesses any solid surface whatsoever upon which a visitor could ever stand. Their dense, turbulent atmosphere contains methane, a gas that selectively absorbs red light and consequently gives both planets their distinctive, shared blue coloration that distinguishes them from other worlds, while temperatures within their swirling upper clouds plunge below a frigid minus 200 degrees Celsius.

Uranus is particularly remarkable among all the planets because it is tilted so dramatically on its rotational axis that it essentially rotates entirely on its side relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun. As the planet travels slowly along its lengthy, elongated orbit, each of its poles experiences roughly 42 consecutive years of continuous, unbroken sunlight, followed immediately by approximately 42 further years of uninterrupted, total darkness.

Because they orbit at such immense distances from the Sun, both planets also possess extraordinarily long years by human standards: Uranus requires 84 full Earth years to complete a single circuit of the Sun, while Neptune requires approximately 165 years to finish just one complete orbital revolution around our star.

Neptune possesses the fastest winds ever reliably measured anywhere within the entire solar system, winds genuinely capable of exceeding 2,000 kilometers per hour within its violently turbulent upper atmosphere.

In 1781, the astronomer William Herschel discovered Uranus using a telescope, making it the very first planet ever identified with the assistance of that particular optical instrument. Subsequently, other astronomers carefully noticed that Uranus was being tugged slightly away from its mathematically predicted orbital path, so they employed rigorous mathematics to calculate precisely where an entirely undiscovered planet might plausibly be located, and in 1846 Neptune was finally observed almost exactly at that calculated position, a genuine triumph of pure scientific reasoning over mere observation alone.

Both planets possess faint, barely visible rings together with numerous orbiting moons of varying sizes. Neptune's largest moon, Triton, orbits in the direction entirely opposite to the planet's own rotation, which is extraordinarily unusual behavior for any large moon in the solar system, and many scientists consequently believe it was originally captured gravitationally from farther out within the solar system. Only a single spacecraft, Voyager 2, has ever visited either world directly, flying past Uranus in 1986 and subsequently past Neptune in 1989, and much of what scientists presently understand about these distant, icy worlds still originates entirely from that single, extraordinary expedition conducted decades ago.

From Herschel's accidental telescope discovery in 1781 to the careful mathematical prediction that led directly to Neptune's observation in 1846, the history of these two tilted, frigid worlds shows just how much of what we currently know about the outer solar system still rests upon a single spacecraft's brief flyby conducted decades in the past.

MID.prompt: How were Uranus and Neptune discovered in different ways? Explain using details from the article.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
MID.modelAnswer: Uranus was discovered in 1781 when the astronomer William Herschel simply pointed his telescope at the sky and noticed it there. Neptune, however, was found in a very different way: astronomers noticed that something was pulling Uranus slightly off its expected orbit, so they used math to predict where an unseen planet must be, and in 1846 Neptune was found almost exactly in that spot. Uranus is also famously tilted on its side, and both ice giants are covered in clouds of methane gas, but scientists only got to see them up close when the Voyager 2 spacecraft flew past them in the 1980s.

HIGH.prompt: Scientists discovered Neptune before anyone saw it. Explain how this happened and why it was an important achievement, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Scientists discovered Neptune before anyone had actually seen it by noticing that Uranus was being pulled slightly away from its expected orbit, as if some unseen planet's gravity were tugging on it. Using mathematics, astronomers predicted almost exactly where this hidden planet should be, and in 1846 Neptune was found right in that location. This was an important achievement because it showed that the invisible atmosphere of a distant world, made largely of methane, could be detected purely through calculation rather than direct observation. It would take well over a century before the Voyager 2 spacecraft finally flew past Neptune in 1989 and confirmed up close what mathematics alone had already predicted.
